title: Memory Concepts
content_html:
Memory Concepts

  1. Predictive processing / Free-energy principle. Treats the brain as a prediction machine that minimizes surprise (free energy), unifying perception, learning, and—by implication—memory as the generative model that underwrites predictions. [1] [2]
  2. Constructive episodic simulation. Episodic memory is adaptive and constructive—its flexibility supports imagining futures by recombining fragments of past events (with the trade-off of distortion). [3] [4]
  3. Temporal Context Models (TCM/CMR). Recollection is guided by a drifting internal context that binds items across time; retrieving one item reinstates its context, cueing neighbors (recency/contiguity, clustering). [5] [6]
  4. Schemas & event segmentation. Prior knowledge (schemas) can accelerate encoding and consolidation, while perceptual ‘event boundaries’ carve experience into episodes that structure memory. [7] [8]
  5. Sleep consolidation & hippocampal replay. Sleep actively stabilizes and reorganizes memories; hippocampal ‘replay’ during sleep re-expresses waking patterns, supporting systems consolidation. [9] [10]
  6. Synaptic tagging & capture (and behavioral tagging). Weakly encoded traces can be ‘rescued’ if they occur near strong events: transient synaptic ‘tags’ capture plasticity-related proteins produced by salient experiences. [11] [12]
  7. Working memory architecture. Beyond a single store: an attentional ‘central executive’ with domain-specific buffers (phonological, visuospatial) and an episodic buffer; capacity often ~3–4 chunks. [13] [14]
  8. Pattern separation & completion. Dentate gyrus/CA3 help keep similar experiences distinct (separation) while enabling retrieval from partial cues (completion)—a core tension in episodic memory. [16]
  9. Attractor-network memory (Hopfield). Content-addressable, error-correcting retrieval emerges from recurrent networks—an influential computational analogy for hippocampal/associative memory. [15]
  10. Metamemory & confidence. Monitoring and control of one’s own memory (e.g., confidence, study choices) have identifiable neural substrates, partly dissociable from task performance. [17] [18] [19]
  11. Biological memories beyond the brain. Adaptive immunity and even innate ‘trained immunity’ show lasting, experience-dependent changes; cells also encode epigenetic ‘memory’ via chromatin marks. [20] [21]
